P1.evidence: The prospect asked directly whether the setter had passed anything over and the answer was no: 'I didn't see any notes anywhere, man. Normally I have them, so I don't know if it just got misplaced or something like that. So unfortunately, I don't have as much context as I'd love to coming in on this call.' A setter did pre-qualify him the previous day, so the check applies and the handoff failed. The frame was the usual three parts plus next steps, agreement was taken with 'Does that all sound good?', and the open question ran.

P2.evidence: The only call in the batch where sleep and energy were actually asked — 'how's your like energy, sleep, stuff like that, mobility?' — and it produced the new job, the 6am start and the six-and-a-half-hour nights. Age, height, weight and work all asked. Current activity asked. Physique satisfaction asked. The injury was probed better than anywhere else in this rep folder: 'how long ago did the shoulder thing happen?', then 'Did you ever end up doing an MRI? Did you ever do physical therapy?' Two failures matter. Diet was never asked at all — the prospect volunteered it in his opening monologue and the rep concluded 'it sounds like you already have nutrition dialed in really well.' And health conditions were never asked, which is why a hereditary clotting disorder surfaced by accident 51 minutes in, during the nutrition pillar, attached to a story about garlic.

P3.evidence: The bridge ran and ran well: 'what's the primary motivation for getting this handled?... what's kind of the drive for this? Like, why is this actually important?' produced the Army PT answer about depression, anxiety and conquering the day. The rep then pushed past the first answer, which is the right instinct: 'So we start this. We start feeling better, having more energy. We feel more confident. We've got the hardest thing out of the way. So then what?' That produced the evolve-until-I-die material and the parking-lot protection answer. He also asked about goals outside fitness, which surfaced the son and the ambition to leave him set. What is missing is the close: no reflect-back at all, and the son — plainly the deepest motivation on the call and someone the prospect wants to train alongside — was never made the centre of the why.

P4.evidence: The trigger question was well put and well timed: 'a year and a half is a long time. And I mean, part of that was probably the healing process. But I'm assuming you've been in a position where you could have started working out and taking it a little bit more seriously... why is it now all of a sudden, what switched in your brain?' The answer was honest — he had been scrolling reels and dismissing the gym as too far. The rest of the phase was thin. Past attempts were not systematically explored, the gap was never named by the prospect in his own words, and the 'why can't you stick to it on your own' challenge was never put, which was reasonable here since the obstacle was a physical injury and geography rather than discipline.

P5.evidence: No cost-of-inaction question at any point. The nearest move was a binary framing rather than a consequence frame: 'do you feel like it is time to draw a line in the sand or do you want to keep scrolling on reels?' The prospect confirmed it — 'I'm not getting any younger. All I'm doing is wasting time. And if I don't start it, I'm wasting time' — which is a good answer the rep did not build on. On a call where the prospect had already lost eighteen months, had a teenage son watching, and had described the injury period as depressive, the two-year question would have written itself.

P6.evidence: The scripted commitment question was never asked before presenting. What ran was a soft temperature check — 'it sounds like we're feeling pretty good about this whole thing. Is that what I'm hearing?' — answered 'Oh, yeah.' The direct version only came after the price and in the middle of arranging payment: 'Dude, you're 10 out of 10, you want to do this, right?' — 'Yeah. Yeah. I need to do it.' The answer was genuine and enthusiastic, so the phase caused no damage here, but it was obtained on the wrong side of the presentation and under time pressure.

P11.evidence: Step 2 ran and ran early — the onboarding call was offered against real availability and booked for 5:15pm Monday with a calendar invite the prospect confirmed receiving. Step 1 failed: no payment was collected, and the reason is worth coaching. The prospect twice offered to spend seven minutes on the phone getting his credit limit raised — 'How much time do you have? I can literally call them, it doesn't take much time' — and the rep twice steered back to taking $2,000 immediately because of his own schedule: 'let's just do the 2K right now. Cause I want to be on time for this call.' The prospect went on hold, a work emergency landed twenty minutes later, and nothing was collected. Steps 3 and 4 were never mentioned at all: no agreement, no welcome email, no Skool link, no onboarding questionnaire. Booking a client into Trevor's calendar before taking any money is its own process risk.

objection_plays.detail: There was no money objection on this call at all — the prospect endorsed the price unprompted as 'an investment that is worth it. 100%.' What existed was a mechanical obstacle: a single credit card with a $2,500 limit and no habit of using credit. The playbook has no branch for a willing buyer who cannot execute payment, so the rep improvised a $2,000-now, $4,000-in-30-days split with an automatic charge. The correct move was almost certainly the one the prospect himself proposed twice — wait seven minutes for the limit increase and take the full $6,000 — and the rep declined it because he had a call queued. A payment-method and payment-capacity branch is missing from the script, and this is the second call in this batch lost to payment mechanics rather than to selling.

Script gap, and the most serious instance of it in the corpus so far: no clinical clearance path. The prospect raised a starting-weight safety question three separate times, disclosed an eighteen-month untreated shoulder injury with no imaging and two refused surgical recommendations, and separately disclosed a hereditary clotting disorder he manages outside conventional medicine. Every instance was routed to 'chat with Trevor on your onboarding call.' There is no screening question, no contraindication list, no clearance requirement and no language for the rep to use, so a rep with no clinical training was left to reassure — 'ideally in like two, three months, it's not even a thing that we have to think about anymore.' The stated ICP has no clinical criterion and the playbook has no clinical play; this call is the clearest argument for both.

notes: Baseline was the best in the batch — the only call where sleep and energy were asked, and the injury history was probed properly — and the two things that were skipped were the two that mattered most: a direct health-conditions question and diet. A clotting disorder surfaced by accident at minute 51 and was never picked up. Commercially this was the easiest deal in the folder, with no objection of any kind, and it did not close because the rep prioritised getting to his next call over letting the prospect spend seven minutes raising his credit limit. Coach two things: ask the health question every time, and never take a partial payment when the full one is seven minutes away.
